lesson.grammar_point: the passive voice in legal and institutional texts

listenings.text: Before we open the reading, I want to clear up the mistake that appears in almost every first essay in this course. Students write that a country signed a treaty and is therefore bound by it. That is not how it works. There are three different moments, and they are often years apart. First, the text is adopted, which means the negotiators agree on the words. Second, it is signed, which shows that a state supports the text. And third, it is ratified, usually after a parliament approves it. Only the third moment creates a legal obligation for that state. And even then, many treaties only enter into force after a minimum number of ratifications. So when you read a headline that says a treaty was signed today, ask yourself one question: signed, or ratified? The answer changes the whole article.

Every time a government threatens to leave an international agreement, our listeners send us the same question: can a country just walk out? The short answer is yes, but not overnight. Most treaties contain their own exit rules, and those rules are usually slower than politicians would like. A written notice has to be sent, and the withdrawal only takes effect after a waiting period, often one year. During that year, the country is still a party, and it is still expected to comply with every provision. Some agreements go further and say that no one can withdraw during the first few years after the treaty enters into force. So when you hear that a country has left an agreement, check the date the notice was given. The country may still be bound for months.

reading.rtitle: A Signature Is Not a Promise
paras: Every year, photographs of heads of state signing a treaty are published around the world, and every year the same mistake is made in the headlines. A signature is treated as the end of the story. In most cases it is only the beginning. When a treaty is signed, a state shows that it agrees with the text, but it is not yet bound by it.

The obligation starts later. In most countries, a treaty has to be approved by the national parliament and then ratified by the government. Only after ratification does a state become a party, and only then is it legally required to comply with every provision it has accepted. Many treaties also say that they will enter into force only when a minimum number of states have ratified them, so a text can be signed by dozens of countries and still have no legal effect for years.

Even then, a state is allowed some room. A reservation can be made at the moment of ratification, stating that one particular article will not be applied. Reservations are not unlimited: one that goes against the object and purpose of the treaty is not accepted. And a state that no longer wants to be bound can withdraw, usually after formal notice has been given.

This is why students of Global Law are often told that the treaty is not the problem. The text is usually clear. The difficult question is what happens after a breach, because in international law there is no police force, and sovereignty is protected by the same system that is supposed to enforce the rules. Most treaties are respected, but they are respected because states choose to, not because anyone can force them.
reading.source: Written for this lesson, from the general rules of treaty law (1969 Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties).

items.situation: A classmate says that a signed treaty is already binding. Correct them in two sentences.
tips: Not yet. A treaty is only binding after it has been ratified, and signing only shows agreement with the text.
Use the passive: has been ratified, is signed.

items.situation: Explain what a reservation is, without using the word reservation.
tips: It is a statement, made when a country ratifies, saying that one article will not be applied to it.
Relative clause plus passive: will not be applied.

items.situation: Say that the treaty was approved by the congress last year, and that it entered into force in May.
tips: The treaty was approved by the congress last year, and it entered into force in May.
Passive for approved; active for entered into force.

items.situation: Your professor asks why international decisions are hard to enforce. Answer in one sentence.
tips: Because there is no international police, and sovereignty is protected by the same system that is supposed to enforce the rules.
Keep it to one sentence, and land on enforce.

items.situation: Tell a friend that a country can leave a treaty, and what it has to do first.
tips: A country can withdraw from a treaty, but formal notice has to be given first.
